newsitem.title: NIGERIA: Nigerian wheat imports seen rising slightly.
newsitem.headline: Nigerian wheat imports seen rising slightly.

text.p: Wheat imports into Nigeria in 1996 are expected to rise slightly to top 650,000 tonnes from below 600,000 tonnes in 1995 but could rise further only if world prices fall significantly, trade sources said on Friday.
"The market is very sluggish at the moment, the increase in prices earlier this year meant flour prices for bakers had to go up," said one importer.
"Those prices have only come down a touch, and we have to hope American prices can come down a good way to really cut prices here and push demand," he added.

Demand for bread flour in Africa's most populous nation is dependent on the purchasing power of the 100 million strong population, which has other staples, such as cassava (manioc), rice, maize and millet to turn to in times of high prices.
By late August when some local crops become more available analysts say it is easier to gauge the extent to which Nigerians are consuming local produce in preference to imported foodstuffs.

Nigerian newspapers have warned that a shortage of fertiliser in maize-growing regions has led farmers to plant other crops this year, but bread would be an unlikely substitute in the face of cheaper alternatives in those areas.
A strengthening local currency may also help importers, although the gains so far are small.
"Easier availability of forex has helped us, and it would be good especially if the naira continues to strengthen, but most of all we are hoping for good harvest reports," said another trade source.
The naira has appreciated from 85 to 80 naira to the dollar in 1996, and from 120 naira to the dollar at the end of 1994.
Local wheat production in Nigeria is unpredictable, but rarely more than a few thousand tonnes.
"The members have not found any wheat to buy locally this year, despite trying very hard," said Gray Longe, spokesman of The Flour Millers Association.
"It seems the total production is being used in the preparation of local foods."
As much as 90 percent of wheat milled in Nigeria is imported from the United States.
Wheat imports in 1994 were estimated as high as 800,000 tonnes.
Installed capacity at the 19 flour mills is almost five million tonnes, but it is years since any of them has run at its potential level.
Nigeria's economy has been mired in recession since a rash of strikes, demonstrations and rapid changes of government policy in the wake of annulled 1993 elections. --Lagos newsroom +234 1 2630317
